Q3630: Capital of Indonesia, on the northwest coast of Java facing the Java Sea; its metro area is called Jabodetabek.
The Dutch East India Company rebuilt it in 1619 as Batavia, its main base in Asia; it was renamed Jakarta during the Japanese occupation.
Indonesian independence was proclaimed here in 1945.
Because Jakarta is sinking and congested, Indonesia is building a new capital, Nusantara, on Borneo.
Q1490: Capital of Japan and seat of the Emperor, at the head of Tokyo Bay on Honshu.
Originally called Edo; it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603 and was renamed Tokyo ('eastern capital') in 1868.
Governed as a prefecture-like 'Metropolis' with 23 special wards, including Shinjuku and Shibuya.
Hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964 and 2021.
Q1354: Capital of Bangladesh, on the Buriganga River in the Ganges Delta; formerly spelled Dacca.
Often called the most densely populated built-up area in the world.
Under the Mughals it was a provincial capital and the hub of the Bengal muslin trade.
The largest Bengali-speaking city in the world.
Q1353: India's National Capital Territory, on the Yamuna River; it contains New Delhi, the seat of government.
Capital of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire for most of the 13th–19th centuries.
Has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort.
Q8686: China's largest city, on the Yangtze estuary, split by the Huangpu River into Puxi and the Pudong skyscraper district.
Its port is the busiest container port in the world.
Opened as a treaty port after the First Opium War (1842); the foreign concessions made it Asia's financial hub in the 1930s.
The Bund waterfront has a row of colonial-era banks and trading houses.
Q987: Capital of India and seat of all three branches of government, inside the larger city of Delhi.
Designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker; the foundation stone was laid by George V in 1911.
Inaugurated as the capital of British India in 1931, replacing Calcutta.
Q16572: Capital of Guangdong on the Pearl River, historically known in the West as Canton.
For a long time the only Chinese port open to European traders, and a terminus of the Maritime Silk Road.
Centre of the Greater Bay Area with Shenzhen, Hong Kong and Macau; home of the Canton Fair, China's biggest trade fair.
Cantonese cuisine and dim sum come from this region.
Q11725: A municipality the size of Austria in southwestern China, at the confluence of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers.
Wartime capital of the Republic of China during the war with Japan (1937–1945).
Known as a 'mountain city' of steep hills, monorails through buildings, and for spicy hot pot.
Separated from Sichuan province in 1997; the Three Gorges Dam reservoir reaches up to it.
Q85: Capital of Egypt near the Nile Delta; Greater Cairo is the largest urban area in Africa and the Arab world.
The Giza pyramids and ancient Memphis lie within the metropolitan area.
Founded in 969 by the Fatimids; called 'the city of a thousand minarets', its historic centre is a World Heritage Site.
Home to Al-Azhar University, one of the oldest universities in the world.
Q1461: Capital of the Philippines, on Manila Bay on the island of Luzon; one of the most densely populated cities proper in the world.
Spanish conquistador Legazpi built the walled city of Intramuros here in 1571.
The Manila galleons linked Asia with Spanish America (Acapulco) for 250 years, making it one of the first global trade cities.
Metro Manila also includes Quezon City, which has more people than Manila itself.
Q174: Brazil's largest city and the most populous city in the Americas, capital of São Paulo state.
Founded by Jesuit priests in 1554; it boomed with the coffee economy in the 19th century.
Brazil's financial centre, with large Italian, Japanese (the biggest community outside Japan) and Lebanese communities.
People from the city are called paulistanos.
Q1489: Capital of Mexico, at 2,240 m in the Valley of Mexico.
Built on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, which stood on an island in Lake Texcoco; the drained lakebed makes the city sink.
Its Zócalo is one of the largest city squares in the world, next to the Metropolitan Cathedral.
Divided into 16 boroughs (alcaldías); has more museums than almost any other city.
Q956: Capital of China, formerly romanized as Peking; the world's most populous national capital.
Seat of emperors of the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties: the Forbidden City and Temple of Heaven are World Heritage Sites.
The Great Wall passes through the mountains north of the city.
The only city to have hosted both the Summer (2008) and Winter (2022) Olympics.
Q1348: Capital of West Bengal on the Hooghly River, known as Calcutta until 2001.
Founded around a British East India Company fort in 1690; capital of British India until 1911.
Often called India's cultural capital: home of Rabindranath Tagore and the Bengal Renaissance.
Landmarks include the Howrah Bridge and the Victoria Memorial; Mother Teresa worked here.
Q8684: Capital of South Korea on the Han River; half of the country's people live in the Seoul metropolitan area.
Capital of the Joseon dynasty for over 500 years, surrounded by the Fortress Wall of Seoul.
Changed hands four times in the Korean War and was rebuilt during the 'Miracle on the Han River'.
Headquarters of Samsung and a centre of K-pop; hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics.
Q1156: Capital of Maharashtra and India's financial capital, on a former archipelago of seven islands; called Bombay until 1995.
Portugal ceded the islands to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry.
Home of Bollywood, the Bombay Stock Exchange, the Gateway of India and the Victorian Gothic Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus.
Dharavi in Mumbai is one of Asia's largest slums.
Q8660: Capital of Sindh and Pakistan's largest city and main seaport, on the Arabian Sea.
Founded as the fishing village of Kolachi in 1729; it grew huge with refugees after the 1947 partition.
Birthplace of Pakistan's founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah, whose mausoleum is a city landmark.
Q60: The largest city in the USA, made of five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island.
Founded by the Dutch as New Amsterdam; renamed New York after the English took it in 1664.
Headquarters of the United Nations and home of Wall Street, the world's largest stock exchanges.
Landmarks: Statue of Liberty, Empire State Building, Central Park, Times Square.
Q35765: Japan's third-largest city, on Osaka Bay; heart of the Keihanshin metro area with Kobe and Kyoto.
Traditionally Japan's merchant and economic hub, nicknamed 'the nation's kitchen'.
Osaka Castle was built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 1580s.
Known for street food such as takoyaki and okonomiyaki; hosted the 1970 and 2025 World Expos.
Q1861: Capital of Thailand on the Chao Phraya River delta; Thais call it Krung Thep ('city of angels').
Became the royal capital in 1782 after Ayutthaya was destroyed; the Grand Palace dates from then.
An extreme primate city: by far Thailand's largest, richest and most important city.
Famous for Buddhist temples like Wat Arun and Wat Pho, canals, and street food.
Q3838: Capital of DR Congo, on the Congo River directly across from Brazzaville, capital of the Republic of the Congo.
Called Léopoldville until 1966, after Belgium's King Leopold II; renamed under Mobutu.
The largest French-speaking city in the world by population.
One of the fastest-growing megacities; the Rumble in the Jungle boxing fight (Ali vs Foreman) was held here in 1974.
Q15174: A city in Guangdong bordering Hong Kong, grown from fishing villages since 1979.
China's first Special Economic Zone under Deng Xiaoping's reforms, often called the 'Silicon Valley of hardware'.
Headquarters of Huawei, Tencent, BYD and DJI; home to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.
Its port is among the busiest container ports in the world.
Q8673: Nigeria's largest city and Africa's most populous urban area, on a lagoon on the Gulf of Guinea.
Capital of Nigeria until 1991, when the government moved to Abuja.
West Africa's financial centre; handles most of Nigeria's exports through its ports.
Centre of Nollywood films and Afrobeats music; the Yoruba name for the city is Èkó.
Q406: Turkey's largest city, on the Bosphorus strait, with parts in both Europe and Asia.
Founded as the Greek colony Byzantium; as Constantinople it was capital of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires.
Conquered by the Ottomans in 1453; Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque and Topkapı Palace are in the old city.
Not the capital: Atatürk moved the capital to Ankara in 1923.
Q1486: Capital of Argentina, on the Río de la Plata estuary; its residents are called porteños ('port people').
Home of the tango, which developed in its working-class neighbourhoods around 1900.
Millions of European immigrants, mostly Italians and Spaniards, arrived from the 19th century onward.
Avenida 9 de Julio, one of the widest avenues in the world, runs past the Obelisk.
Q30002: Capital of Sichuan province in western China, on the fertile Chengdu Plain ('Land of Abundance').
Home of the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
Kept the same name for over 2,000 years; capital of the Shu Han kingdom in the Three Kingdoms era.
A UNESCO City of Gastronomy, famous for spicy, numbing Sichuan pepper cuisine; the ancient Dujiangyan irrigation system is nearby.
Q11739: Capital of Punjab province and Pakistan's second-largest city, near the Indian border.
A Mughal capital: the Badshahi Mosque, Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens date from that era.
Capital of the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh in the early 19th century.
The 1940 Lahore Resolution called for the creation of Pakistan.
Q11736: Large port city on the Bohai Sea, about 120 km southeast of Beijing, which it serves as a sea gateway.
A treaty port from 1860 with nine foreign concessions; their European-style buildings still stand.
One of China's four municipalities directly under the central government.
Badly damaged by the 1976 Tangshan earthquake.
Q649: Capital of Russia on the Moskva River; the largest city entirely in Europe.
First mentioned in 1147; the Grand Principality of Moscow unified the Russian lands.
Peter the Great moved the capital to Saint Petersburg in 1712; the Bolsheviks moved it back in 1918.
The Kremlin and Red Square with St Basil's Cathedral are World Heritage Sites; its Metro stations are famous for their decoration.
Q1355: Capital of Karnataka on the Deccan Plateau at about 900 m; known as Bangalore until 2014.
India's 'Silicon Valley': the centre of the Indian IT industry, home to Infosys and Wipro.
Founded as a mud fort by Kempe Gowda I in 1537; nicknamed the 'Garden City'.
Has many aerospace and research institutions, including ISRO, India's space agency.
Q1854: Vietnam's largest city and economic centre, on the Saigon River; called Saigon until 1976.
Capital of South Vietnam until its fall in April 1975, which ended the Vietnam War.
Renamed after Ho Chi Minh, the leader of North Vietnam.
Landmarks include the Independence Palace, the War Remnants Museum and Bến Thành Market.
Q8678: Brazil's second-largest city, between mountains and the Atlantic; nicknamed the 'Marvellous City'.
Capital of Brazil until 1960 (when Brasília took over); from 1808 to 1821 it was also seat of the Portuguese royal court.
Christ the Redeemer statue, Sugarloaf Mountain, Copacabana and Ipanema beaches.
Famous for its Carnival and samba; hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics; residents are called cariocas.
Q65: The second-largest city in the USA, in Southern California on the Pacific coast.
Centre of the global film and TV industry: Hollywood is a neighbourhood of the city.
Founded as a Spanish pueblo in 1781 and part of Mexico until 1848.
Known for sprawl and freeways; hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984 and will again in 2028.
Q1050826: The metropolitan region around Los Angeles, spanning five Southern California counties.
Centre of the global entertainment industry: film, television and recorded music.
Includes Long Beach, Anaheim (home of Disneyland), Santa Ana and the Inland Empire.
The Port of Los Angeles and Port of Long Beach together are the busiest port complex in the USA.
Q1352: Capital of Tamil Nadu on the Bay of Bengal coast; known as Madras until 1996.
Grew around Fort St. George, the first British fortress in India, built in 1644.
Its municipal corporation (1688) is the oldest in India.
A centre of Tamil cinema ('Kollywood'), Carnatic music and India's car industry ('Detroit of India').
Q11746: Capital of Hubei at the confluence of the Yangtze and the Han rivers.
Formed from three towns: Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang.
The 1911 Wuchang Uprising here began the revolution that ended imperial rule in China.
COVID-19 was first identified here in December 2019, followed by the first lockdown of the pandemic.
Q4970: Capital of Zhejiang province, at the southern end of the Grand Canal; one of China's Eight Ancient Capitals.
Capital of the Southern Song dynasty; Marco Polo described it as one of the finest cities in the world.
Its West Lake is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and famous in Chinese poetry and painting.
Headquarters of Alibaba, Geely and DeepSeek; hosted the 2022 Asian Games.
Q2841: Capital of Colombia, high in the Andes at about 2,600 m.
Founded in 1538 by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada on land of the Muisca people; capital of the Viceroyalty of New Granada.
Capital of Gran Colombia after Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in 1819.
Known for the Gold Museum and the TransMilenio bus rapid transit system.
Q2868: Capital of Peru, in a coastal desert on the Pacific; one of the driest capitals in the world.
Founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 as the 'City of Kings'; capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru.
Its historic centre is a World Heritage Site; it includes the port of Callao.
Known as a capital of Latin American cuisine, e.g. ceviche.
Q3897: Capital and main seaport of Angola, on the Atlantic coast.
Founded by the Portuguese in 1576; for centuries a centre of the slave trade to Brazil.
The largest Portuguese-speaking city outside Brazil.
Grew rapidly with refugees from the Angolan Civil War (1975–2002); later boomed with oil money.
Q90: Capital of France on the Seine, nicknamed the 'City of Light'.
Divided into 20 arrondissements; Haussmann's 19th-century boulevards shaped the modern city.
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum; other landmarks are the Eiffel Tower and Notre-Dame.
Hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
Q1361: Capital of Telangana on the Deccan Plateau, along the Musi River.
Founded in 1591 by the Qutb Shahi dynasty; the Charminar monument dates from that year.
For centuries ruled by the Nizams, once among the richest men in the world; joined India in 1948.
A big IT and pharma centre ('Cyberabad') and home of the Telugu film industry; known for Hyderabadi biryani.
Q5826: Capital of Shaanxi province; known as Chang'an, it was the capital of the Zhou, Qin, Han, Sui and Tang dynasties.
The eastern starting point of the Silk Road.
The Terracotta Army of the first Qin emperor was found just outside the city in 1974.
Has one of the best-preserved city walls in China.
Q59218: Industrial city in the Pearl River Delta between Guangzhou and Shenzhen.
Known as 'the world's factory', a huge exporter of electronics, toys, textiles and furniture.
Home of the New South China Mall, one of the largest shopping malls in the world.
The 1839 burning of opium at Humen, a cause of the First Opium War, happened in Dongguan.
Q84: Capital of the United Kingdom, on the River Thames; the largest metro area in Western Europe.
Founded by the Romans as Londinium; the medieval 'City of London' is now the financial district.
In the 19th century it was the largest city in the world, capital of the British Empire.
Big Ben, the Tower of London, Buckingham Palace; the only city to have hosted three Summer Olympics (1908, 1948, 2012).
Q16666: Capital of Jiangsu on the Yangtze; the name means 'southern capital'.
Capital of several Chinese dynasties and of the Republic of China; Sun Yat-sen's mausoleum is here.
Site of the Nanjing Massacre by Japanese troops in 1937–38.
Its Ming-dynasty city wall is one of the longest surviving city walls in the world.
Q1949403: City in Bihar on the north bank of the Ganges, opposite Patna.
Linked to Patna by the Mahatma Gandhi Setu, a 5.75 km bridge across the Ganges.
Known for its banana plantations; headquarters of Vaishali district, an ancient Buddhist site.
Q3616: Capital of Iran, at the foot of the Alborz mountains; the largest city in West Asia.
Made capital in 1786 by the Qajar dynasty; it is the 51st capital in Iran's history.
Nearby ancient Rey (Rhages) is now part of the metro area.
Landmarks include the Golestan Palace, the Azadi Tower and the Milad Tower.
Q11751: Capital of Aichi Prefecture in central Honshu; its seaport is the largest in Japan.
Centre of Japan's car industry: Toyota is headquartered nearby in Toyota City.
Nagoya Castle, rebuilt after WWII, is known for its golden shachihoko (tiger-fish) roof ornaments.
On the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Osaka.
Q34412: Prefecture-level city in Guangdong, merged into one urban area with Guangzhou in the Pearl River Delta.
Regarded as the home of Cantonese opera, southern Chinese kung fu and lion dancing.
Hometown of Wong Fei-hung, the martial artist made famous by Jackie Chan and Jet Li films.
A big manufacturing centre for ceramics, furniture and household appliances (Midea).
